title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Nonodontogenic cysts originate from tissues not involved in tooth formation and are predominantly developmental in nature. These lesions are uncommon but may be encountered by dental and medical professionals during routine oral examinations. Etiologic factors include aberrant epithelial remnants and congenital tissue malformations. Risk factors remain poorly defined, although certain cysts demonstrate a predilection for specific age groups or anatomical sites.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Nonodontogenic cysts develop through epithelial proliferation and fluid accumulation, leading to localized expansion. Clinically, they may present as asymptomatic swellings, mucosal elevations, or radiolucent lesions on imaging.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Diagnosis requires thorough clinical assessment, radiographic evaluation, and histopathologic confirmation, with particular attention to excluding odontogenic origin due to differences in management. Treatment typically involves surgical enucleation or marsupialization, depending on size and location. Complications may include infection, adjacent structure displacement, or recurrence. Prognosis is generally favorable following complete excision, with minimal risk of long-term sequelae.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to sharpen learners' skills in evaluating and managing nonodontogenic cysts. Participants will deepen their understanding of the condition's etiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic recommendations. Enhanced competence will empower clinicians to collaborate with interprofessional teams providing care for individuals with these oral growths.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify the clinical and diagnostic features of nonodontogenic cysts, including accurate classification to guide therapeutic strategies. Implement evidence-based, individualized approaches for managing nonodontogenic cysts. Improve patient understanding of nonodontogenic cysts, including causes, symptoms, treatment options, and expected outcomes, to ensure management adherence. title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Introduction
content: Nonodontogenic cysts of the oral cavity constitute a heterogeneous group of epithelium-lined lesions arising from tissues not involved in tooth formation. Many of these growths are asymptomatic and identified incidentally during routine clinical or radiographic evaluation. However, presentation, histopathology, and management vary considerably. Most nonodontogenic cysts are developmental, arising from persistent remnants of embryonic epithelial structures that later contribute to cyst formation.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Introduction
content: Although typically benign, these lesions warrant clinical recognition. The masses can resemble odontogenic cysts, inflammatory swellings, or neoplasms, and misdiagnosis may result in inappropriate intervention or delayed identification of pathology. Early and accurate detection is essential to guide management and inform patient counseling.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Introduction
content: This activity addresses 5 clinically significant nonodontogenic cysts: the nasopalatine duct cyst, nasolabial cyst, palatal cyst of the neonate, oral lymphoepithelial cyst, and epidermoid cyst. The epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnostic evaluation, and management strategies are presented, emphasizing precise diagnosis for optimal patient outcomes.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Etiology -- Nasopalatine Duct Cyst
content: The nasopalatine duct cyst is the most common nonodontogenic cyst, typically presenting as a radiolucent lesion in the anterior maxilla, often with a characteristic heart-shaped appearance on radiographs. Clinically, this anomalous structure may manifest as a painless swelling of the anterior palate (see Image . Nasopalatine Duct Cyst). Nasopalatine duct cysts originate from epithelial remnants of the nasopalatine duct. [1] Factors contributing to the development of these cysts include infection, trauma, or mucous retention.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Etiology -- Nasolabial Cyst
content: Nasolabial cysts manifest as soft, fluctuant swellings in the nasolabial fold, potentially causing cosmetic deformity or nasal obstruction. Two principal hypotheses explain the pathogenesis of these lesions. One suggests formation from retained epithelial cells within the mesenchyme following fusion of the nasal processes, while the other proposes derivation from epithelial remnants of the nasolacrimal duct at the junction of the nasal process and maxillary prominence. Definitive confirmation of these mechanisms has yet to be provided. [2]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Etiology -- Palatal Cysts of the Neonate
content: Palatal cysts of the neonate, also referred to as "Epstein pearls" or "Bohn nodules," present as small, white-to-yellow nodules along the palatal midline or at the junction of the hard and soft palate. These lesions arise from keratin entrapment within palatal tissue, resulting in cystic formation. [3] Epstein pearls are located along the median palatal raphe, whereas Bohn nodules are distributed over the hard palate.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Etiology -- Oral Lymphoepithelial Cyst
content: Oral lymphoepithelial cysts typically appear as small, yellowish nodules with a smooth surface, most commonly on the floor of the mouth or lateral tongue. Pathogenesis is most commonly attributed to the association with oral lymphoid tissue (Waldeyer ring) and the entrapment or accumulation of desquamated epithelial cells within dilated crypts. [4]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Etiology -- Epidermoid Cyst
content: Epidermoid cysts usually present as slow-growing, painless masses, most frequently on the floor of the mouth. These inclusion cysts originate from ectoderm and may also develop secondary to trauma, which displaces epithelial tissue into deeper layers, where proliferation forms a cystic cavity. [5]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Epidemiology -- Nasopalatine Duct Cyst
content: Nasopalatine duct cysts are the most common nonodontogenic cysts of the anterior maxilla. [6] A 3:1 male predilection has been reported, although cyst size does not correlate with patient sex. [7] The mean age at presentation is 47 years. [8]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Epidemiology -- Nasolabial Cyst
content: Nasolabial cysts are uncommon, accounting for approximately 0.7% of all maxillofacial cysts. [9] These lesions predominantly affect women in the 4th to 5th decades, with a mean age of 51 years.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Epidemiology -- Palatal Cysts of the Neonate
content: Palatal cysts of the neonate occur in 60% to 85% of newborns, with no sex predilection. [10] Incidence is higher in term infants compared to postterm births. [11]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Epidemiology -- Oral Lymphoepithelial Cyst
content: Oral lymphoepithelial cysts are rare and demonstrate no sex predilection. [12] These growths are usually associated with lymphoid tissue of the Waldeyer ring, including the palatine and lingual tonsils and pharyngeal adenoids. Incidence ranges from 1.2% to 7%, with a mean presentation age of 44 years. [13]

content: Intraoral epidermoid cysts are uncommon, with a male predilection. [14] The mean age at presentation is 28 years.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Pathophysiology -- Nasopalatine Duct Cyst
content: Nasopalatine duct cysts originate from epithelial remnants of the nasopalatine duct, which may be activated by trauma, infection, or spontaneously. These developmental or reactive structures can expand over time, forming intraosseous cavities in the anterior maxilla.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Pathophysiology -- Nasolabial Cyst
content: The pathogenesis of the nasolabial cyst remains incompletely defined. Current evidence suggests that epithelial remnants of the nasolacrimal duct undergo spontaneous activation, resulting in cystic expansion. These growths often develop gradually and remain asymptomatic until they produce aesthetic deformity or functional impairment.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Pathophysiology -- Palatal Cysts of the Neonate
content: Palatal cysts of the newborn arise from entrapped epithelium during fusion of the palatal processes or from minor salivary gland tissue. Residual epithelial clefts may persist during closure of the palatal shelves at 10 to 11 weeks of gestation, forming keratin-filled cavities. Epstein pearls are located along the median palatal raphe, whereas Bohn nodules are distributed near the junction of the hard and soft palate.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Pathophysiology -- Oral Lymphoepithelial Cyst
content: Oral lymphoepithelial cysts develop from epithelial remnants entrapped within the lymphoid tissue of the Waldeyer ring or from obstruction of minor salivary gland ducts. [15] Obstruction of a salivary duct results in continued secretion, leading to accumulation and formation of a cystic structure, which may become inflamed.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Pathophysiology -- Epidermoid Cyst
content: Epidermoid cysts originate from epidermal inclusions and are distinguished from dermoid cysts by the absence of skin adnexa, such as sebaceous glands or hair follicles. [16] These inclusions progressively form cystic cavities, culminating in the development of an epidermoid cystic lesion.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Histopathology -- Nasopalatine Duct Cyst
content: Nasopalatine duct cysts are histologically characterized by a cystic lining of flattened stratified squamous epithelium, approximately 2 to 3 cell layers thick. [17] The lumen may contain proteinaceous fluid or cellular debris, reflecting cystic activity.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Histopathology -- Nasolabial Cyst
content: Histologically, nasolabial cysts are lined by epithelium ranging from stratified squamous to ciliated pseudostratified columnar types. [18] Scattered mucous or goblet cells are commonly observed within the epithelial lining, contributing to secretory activity.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Histopathology -- Palatal Cysts of the Neonate
content: Palatal cysts of the newborn exhibit a keratin-filled lumen lined by stratified squamous epithelium. The cystic content is typically acellular keratin, reflecting the benign and developmental nature of these lesions.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Histopathology -- Oral Lymphoepithelial Cyst
content: Oral lymphoepithelial cysts are lined by stratified squamous epithelium and surrounded by dense lymphoid tissue. The encapsulation by lymphoid follicles distinguishes these cysts from other oral cystic lesions.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Histopathology -- Epidermoid Cyst
content: Epidermoid cysts display a cystic wall composed of stratified squamous epithelium devoid of skin adnexa. The lumen is filled with abundant keratin flakes, which accumulate as the cyst slowly enlarges over time. [19]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- History and Physical -- Nasopalatine Duct Cyst
content: Nasopalatine duct cysts appear as well-circumscribed radiolucencies in the anterior maxilla. Superimposition of the nasal spine often produces a characteristic heart-shaped appearance on radiographs (see Image . Nasopalatine Duct Cyst on Radiography). Clinically, these lesions may present as firm, painless swellings of the anterior hard palate, frequently crossing the midline, with or without drainage.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- History and Physical -- Nasolabial Cyst
content: Nasolabial cysts manifest as asymptomatic swellings in the nasolabial region of the midface, typically ranging from 1 to 5 cm in diameter. [20] These lesions are soft and fluctuant on palpation. Patients may report nasal obstruction or aesthetic concerns associated with lesion expansion.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- History and Physical -- Palatal Cysts of the Neonate
content: Palatal cysts of the neonate present as small, white-to-yellow nodules adjacent to the palatal midline. [21] These cystic structures are firm on palpation and generally measure a few millimeters in diameter. These growths may occur as solitary or cluster lesions along the median palatal raphe (see Image . Palatal Cysts of the Newborn).

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- History and Physical -- Oral Lymphoepithelial Cyst
content: Oral lymphoepithelial cysts present as yellowish-white nodules with smooth surfaces. These cysts most commonly occur on the ventral surface or lateral borders of the tongue or the floor of the mouth but may be identified on any oral mucosal site associated with lymphoid tissue of the Waldeyer ring (see Image . Lymphoepithelial Cysts on the Posterior Pharyngeal Pillar).

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- History and Physical -- Epidermoid Cyst
content: Epidermoid cysts typically manifest on the floor of the mouth as asymptomatic, slow-growing masses. [22] These lesions are firm yet fluctuant on palpation and are often not detected until they attain a significant size (see Image . Epidermoid Cyst on Lateral Tongue). A historical female predilection has been reported. [23]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Evaluation -- Nasopalatine Duct Cyst
content: Nasopalatine duct cysts are histologically characterized by an epithelium-lined cyst wall surrounded by fibrovascular connective tissue, with occasional minor salivary glands present as incidental findings. [24] Vitality testing of adjacent teeth is essential to exclude an odontogenic origin, such as a periapical cyst or granuloma, as teeth associated with a nasopalatine duct cyst typically remain vital.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Evaluation -- Nasolabial Cyst
content: Nasolabial cysts exhibit a cystic lining of pseudostratified columnar epithelium, with occasional areas of stratified squamous epithelium. [25] Diagnosis is established by correlating these histopathologic features with the clinical presentation. [26]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Evaluation -- Palatal Cysts of the Neonate
content: Palatal cysts of the neonate are diagnosed primarily based on clinical examination, obviating the need for additional laboratory or imaging studies. These lesions are typically self-limiting and identifiable by their characteristic appearance along the palatal midline.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Evaluation -- Oral Lymphoepithelial Cyst
content: Oral lymphoepithelial cysts present as cystic structures lined by stratified squamous epithelium and encapsulated by lymphoid tissue. [27] Nuclear atypia is generally absent, supporting the benign developmental nature of these growths. [28]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Evaluation -- Epidermoid Cyst
content: Epidermoid cysts are histologically lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium without dermal appendages within the surrounding fibrous connective tissue. Advanced imaging modalities, such as computed tomography scans, may demonstrate these lesions as well-circumscribed, unilocular, low-density masses, aiding in preoperative assessment.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Treatment / Management -- Nasopalatine Duct Cyst
content: Nasopalatine duct cysts are optimally managed through surgical resection. Postoperative monitoring with both clinical examination and radiographic imaging is recommended to ensure complete resolution. Recurrence following complete excision is uncommon. [29]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Treatment / Management -- Nasolabial Cyst
content: Nasolabial cysts are generally treated by conservative surgical excision. These lesions demonstrate a low recurrence rate following complete removal.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Treatment / Management -- Palatal Cysts of the Neonate
content: Palatal cysts of the neonate are self-limiting and typically rupture spontaneously. Parents should be reassured that the lesions resolve naturally, and recurrence is rare.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Treatment / Management -- Oral Lymphoepithelial Cyst
content: Oral lymphoepithelial cysts may be managed by conservative surgical excision. Recurrence is not expected after complete removal of the cystic structure.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Treatment / Management -- Epidermoid Cyst
content: Epidermoid cysts are treated by conservative surgical enucleation. Complete excision generally prevents recurrence, which is infrequent.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Accurate differentiation of nonodontogenic cysts from other oral pathologies is critical due to overlapping clinical and imaging characteristics. The differentials listed for each cyst type below include conditions with similar location, appearance, or histopathology: Nasopalatine duct cysts Any odontogenic cyst (lateral periodontal cyst and periapical cyst or granuloma) Enlarged incisive fossa Central giant cell granuloma Nasolabial cyst Radicular cyst Periapical abscess Nasopalatine duct cyst Benign mesenchymal tumors Minor salivary gland tumors Palatal cysts of the newborn Congenital epulis Dental lamina cysts Natal tooth Oral Lymphoepithelial Cyst Branchial cleft cyst Lipoma Mucocele Sialolithiasis Epidermoid Cyst Lipoma Dermoid cyst Oral lymphoepithelial cyst Benign mesenchymal tumors

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Timely and precise identification of nonodontogenic cysts allows clinicians across disciplines to implement targeted management strategies. Involving patients and families in discussions of lesion characteristics, treatment expectations, and follow-up promotes adherence and reduces anxiety.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Prognosis
content: All 5 nonodontogenic cysts generally have a favorable prognosis. Nasopalatine duct cysts rarely recur, and histopathology typically confirms complete excision. Nasolabial cysts are curative with complete surgical removal, and palatal cysts of the newborn resolve spontaneously within weeks to months. Oral lymphoepithelial cysts are benign, with no reported recurrences following excision. Epidermoid cysts also have a favorable prognosis, and complete surgical removal usually prevents recurrence. [30]
contents: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Prognosis. All 5 nonodontogenic cysts generally have a favorable prognosis. Nasopalatine duct cysts rarely recur, and histopathology typically confirms complete excision. Nasolabial cysts are curative with complete surgical removal, and palatal cysts of the newborn resolve spontaneously within weeks to months. Oral lymphoepithelial cysts are benign, with no reported recurrences following excision. Epidermoid cysts also have a favorable prognosis, and complete surgical removal usually prevents recurrence. [30]

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Complications
content: Nasopalatine duct cysts may demonstrate expansile growth, and in rare cases, intraoral drainage can occur. These lesions arise from epithelial remnants of the nasopalatine duct, with activation potentially triggered by mucous retention, trauma, or infection, which may produce pain or pressure as the cyst enlarges. [31] However, most cysts are clinically silent with nonspecific features and may evade detection during routine clinical or radiographic evaluation.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Complications
content: Nasolabial cysts can mimic both nonodontogenic and odontogenic lesions clinically. Consequently, histopathological examination is essential for definitive diagnosis. Palatal cysts of the newborn typically undergo spontaneous rupture and resolve without associated complications. Oral lymphoepithelial cysts rarely result in complications following surgical excision, and recurrence is not observed.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Complications
content: Epidermoid cysts that attain larger dimensions may lead to functional complications, including difficulty with speech or respiration. [32] These lesions are often clinically unrecognized until significant growth or symptom development prompts evaluation.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: All 5 nonodontogenic cysts discussed are developmental in origin, and, consequently, no preventative measures are available. Nasopalatine duct cysts may be detected incidentally on radiographs, and patients should be informed of any findings and counseled regarding biopsy to exclude other lesions. Nasolabial cysts similarly arise from developmental remnants, and patients should be advised that recurrence following complete surgical excision is rare.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Palatal cysts of the newborn are self-limiting. Parents should be reassured that these lesions resolve spontaneously over time without intervention. Oral lymphoepithelial cysts, arising from entrapped epithelium within lymphoid tissue, require excision, and patients should be informed about the procedure and expected outcomes. Epidermoid cysts are predominantly developmental, and conservative surgical removal typically ensures complete resolution.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Although generally benign, nonodontogenic cysts constitute an important diagnostic category of oral lesions. The clinical and radiographic features of these growths may overlap with odontogenic cysts, inflammatory conditions, and neoplastic pathology, making accurate identification essential for guiding patient management. A comprehensive evaluation integrating clinical examination, imaging, and histopathologic assessment is critical for establishing the correct diagnosis.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: These cysts may be encountered by dentists, oral surgeons, pediatricians, otolaryngologists, and other healthcare professionals, highlighting the importance of interprofessional collaboration in optimizing patient outcomes. Clinicians should maintain a broad differential diagnosis, recognize indications for biopsy or referral, and communicate findings effectively to the broader care team.

title: Non-Odontogenic Cysts -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Most nonodontogenic cysts have a favorable prognosis and are successfully managed through conservative surgical excision or, in selected cases, observation alone. Educating patients and families regarding the benign nature and anticipated course of these lesions supports adherence, reduces anxiety, and fosters trust in the treatment plan. Coordinated care across specialties ensures timely diagnosis, appropriate management, and reassurance for patients presenting with these lesions.
